name: BuiltWith
tagline: Detects the technologies behind websites and sells the results as lead lists
team: Solo founder (Gary Brewer) plus a non-operating co-founder/advisor (Andrew Rogers) and a content contractor, per 2015 coverage; later reported as one employee
summary: BuiltWith crawls the web, detects which technologies each site uses (CMS, analytics, ecommerce platform, CDN and so on), and sells searchable lists of those sites. The main buyers are sales and marketing teams who want leads filtered by technology. The ~$14M/yr figure was spread by Nathan Barry in 2022 and is widely repeated (Starter Story now estimates more), but BuiltWith has never published audited financials.
origin: In 2007 Gary Brewer was visiting startup sites and viewing their source to see what they were built with. No tool automated that, so he built one. He worked on it every evening for about four years while holding a full-time job, and by the time Andrew Rogers met him in 2011 it was already making about $40,000 a month.
howItMakesMoney: Monthly subscriptions to the full dataset: Basic $295/mo, Pro $495/mo, Team $995/mo, with annual billing at ten times the monthly price. Individual site lookups are free. In 2015 Brewer told Startup Daily it had 'a few thousand' paying users (2,000 to 3,000), split about 40% Basic, 40% Pro and 20% Enterprise.
growth: A free single-site lookup ('what is this site built with?') brings in large organic traffic. In 2015 Startup Daily reported 500,000+ users and about 2M page views a month, with no outbound sales team.
Users started asking for lists, such as Australian sites on a CDN or stores running Magento. Answering those requests turned a curiosity tool into a lead-generation product.
The crawl data compounds. Historical records of when a site added or dropped a technology are hard for a newcomer to recreate.
Pricing is a few high tiers aimed at B2B sales teams who can easily justify $300-1,000 a month, not at many low-price consumers.
moat: More than 15 years of crawl history and technology-detection rules, plus the organic search traffic a lookup tool with that much history earns. A new competitor can detect technologies today but cannot go back and create the historical adoption and churn data.
risks: Competitors (Wappalyzer, SimilarTech, HG Insights) and cheap in-house detection with headless browsers push prices down. Lead-list data also depends on privacy and scraping rules staying roughly where they are.

timeline.event: BuiltWith launches as a side project in Australia
Brewer works on it evenings for about four years while holding a full-time job
Andrew Rogers meets Brewer, finds it making ~$40k/month, encourages him to go full time and joins for equity with a 'Co-Founder' title
Startup Daily reports 2,000-3,000 paying customers and no staff
Nathan Barry spreads the '$14M a year with one employee' figure

lessons: A free lookup tool can serve as the SEO engine, while the paid product is the same data sold in bulk.
Watch what power users ask for. BuiltWith's lead-list business came from people emailing to ask for exports.
Price B2B data by the value of the leads it produces (hundreds of dollars a month), not by what it costs to build.
Data that builds up over time, such as history and change logs, is a stronger moat than a one-time scrape.

rebuild.idea: An 'AI stack' detector that shows which LLM providers, vector databases and agent frameworks companies use, drawn from JS bundles, DNS/CNAMEs, status-page vendors and job posts, and sold as lead lists to AI tooling vendors.
rebuild.why: BuiltWith-style detectors are built around front-end technology fingerprints. Most AI adoption happens on the backend and is only visible through indirect signals such as job posts, subprocessor lists and SDK traces.
mvp: Pick 30 signals, such as OpenAI/Anthropic SDK strings in public JS, Pinecone/Weaviate hostnames, and 'LangChain' in job posts
Crawl 50k B2B SaaS domains plus their careers and subprocessor pages, and store results with timestamps
Publish a free 'what AI does X use?' lookup page per company for SEO
Sell a $199/mo CSV export filtered by signal to 3-5 AI infrastructure startups, found through LinkedIn outreach to their growth leads
rebuild.fit: A data engineer comfortable with crawling, entity resolution and scheduled pipelines
rebuild.pricing: Free per-company lookups for SEO, then $199/mo for filtered CSV exports and $499/mo for CRM sync and weekly change alerts.
rebuild.market: Buyers are growth and sales teams at AI infrastructure and devtool startups, reached through LinkedIn outreach, the free lookup pages and data posts on X. Competitors are BuiltWith, Wappalyzer, HG Insights, Apollo and Clay's technographic enrichments.

name: The Saturday Solopreneur + courses
tagline: Newsletter and self-paced courses on building a one-person internet business
summary: Justin Welsh is a former SaaS sales executive who sells self-paced courses (The LinkedIn Operating System, The Content Operating System, The Creator MBA) to an audience built on LinkedIn and X, funneled through a weekly newsletter. He reported $4.15M+ in 2024 revenue at about 86% margins without employees.
origin: Welsh was a revenue executive at healthcare SaaS company PatientPop and left after burnout in 2019. He started posting daily on LinkedIn about sales and growth, did some advising, and turned his LinkedIn process into a course. He pre-sold The LinkedIn Operating System in July 2021, about 30 days before it went live.
howItMakesMoney: One-time-purchase digital courses sold from his own site and Gumroad. The LinkedIn Operating System has been listed at around $150-$200. The free Saturday newsletter (started January 2022) is the main funnel into the courses and later The Creator MBA bundle.
growth: Posted on LinkedIn and X daily for years, repurposing the same ideas across both platforms
Pre-sold the LinkedIn course in July 2021 to validate demand before building it
Launched The Saturday Solopreneur newsletter in January 2022; reported roughly 77K subscribers after one year
Published revenue and margin numbers openly, which itself became shareable content
Added higher-priced bundles (The Creator MBA) sold to the existing newsletter list
moat: A very large personal following on LinkedIn and X plus a newsletter list, both tied to his personal story. Buyers are paying for his specific system and credibility, which a copycat course can't easily replicate.
risks: Revenue depends on one person's attention and on platform algorithms (LinkedIn, X). The 'how to grow an audience' course market is crowded and prone to saturation.

timeline.event: Leaves PatientPop executive role after burnout; starts posting daily on LinkedIn
Pre-sells The LinkedIn Operating System 30 days before launch
Starts The Saturday Solopreneur newsletter
Reported ~$1.7M revenue for the year
Reports $4.15M+ revenue at ~86% margins; launches two new products

lessons: Pre-sell a course before building it; a 30-day pre-sale gives both validation and a deadline
Build the audience on one or two platforms with daily posting before expecting product sales
Use a free newsletter as the owned channel that turns social followers into buyers
Keep costs low (no staff, off-the-shelf tools) so most revenue becomes profit
Productize your prior career skill (sales, growth) rather than a topic you are new to

rebuild.idea: A course and newsletter teaching licensed tradespeople (electricians, HVAC techs) to leave employment and run a one-van business, built from one tradesperson's own numbers
rebuild.why: Solopreneur education is aimed almost entirely at knowledge workers; trades have high demand and few people teaching the business side in plain language.
mvp: Post daily on LinkedIn/Facebook trade groups about your own pricing, quoting and client numbers
Collect emails with a free quoting spreadsheet
Pre-sell a $99 'first 90 days solo' course to the list with a 30-day delivery date
Deliver it as 6-8 recorded screen shares plus templates
rebuild.fit: A working tradesperson who already runs their own small shop and is comfortable posting publicly

name: HeadshotPro
tagline: AI-generated professional headshots for individuals and remote teams
team: Solo founder (a small team is reported later)
summary: HeadshotPro turns a set of selfies into studio-style corporate headshots and sells one-time packs to individuals and companies. Danny Postma launched it in March 2023, forking it from his earlier ProfilePicture.AI. It is widely reported at around $300k/month, but no primary source for that figure could be accessed.
origin: Postma, a Dutch indie developer who had earlier built and sold the AI copywriting tool Headlime, launched ProfilePicture.AI in late 2022, reportedly built in about 30 hours. He then forked it into HeadshotPro (March 2023), aimed at a narrower and more commercial job: professional headshots for remote teams and LinkedIn profiles. He later said HeadshotPro was thriving while ProfilePictureAI was dying.
howItMakesMoney: One-time packs rather than subscriptions: reported tiers of about $29 (40 headshots), $39 (100) and $59 (200). Companies buy team packages so remote staff get matching headshots. An affiliate program pays partners a commission, which Danny advertised at 20% of sales.
growth: SEO: Postma is known for SEO-first building and targeted 'AI headshots' and 'professional headshots' search intent. Indie Hackers analysed this strategy as driving $300k+ in the first year.
Affiliates: Rewardful published a case study of HeadshotPro earning $50k+ monthly through affiliate marketing.
Positioned for B2B team orders (consistent headshots for remote companies), which raises order value compared with individual buyers.
Launch promotion on X and TikTok, including a $1,000 bonus for the first creators whose videos passed 100K views.
moat: Search rankings for high-intent terms, a large affiliate network and B2B team accounts are harder to copy than the underlying model pipeline.
risks: General image models increasingly produce convincing headshots for free. Paid search and SEO competition for 'AI headshots' is intense, and results depend on Google's ranking decisions.

timeline.event: Launches ProfilePicture.AI, an earlier AI avatar and photo product
Launches HeadshotPro for professional headshots for remote teams
Starts an affiliate program at 20% of sales with TikTok creator bonuses
Widely reported at ~$300k/month; the Rewardful case study cites $50k+/month from affiliates
Postma notes HeadshotPro (thriving) is a fork of ProfilePictureAI (dying)

lessons: Narrow the use case until it has a budget. 'Headshots for work' beats 'fun AI avatars'.
Fork a declining product into a more commercial niche instead of starting from scratch.
One-time packs match a one-time need and avoid churn and cancellation complaints.
Affiliates and SEO together can replace a sales team for a consumer and B2B hybrid.

rebuild.idea: AI-generated, brand-consistent staff photos for small healthcare and real-estate practices, delivered as ready-to-upload website 'Meet the team' pages and Google Business Profile images.
rebuild.why: Headshot tools stop at the image file. Small practices still pay a photographer and a web designer to get consistent team pages.
mvp: Pick one vertical (e.g. dental clinics) and hand-build 3 sample team pages using existing headshot APIs.
Cold-email 100 clinics whose websites have mismatched or missing team photos, offering a $199 flat package.
Deliver the first 5 orders by hand to learn the edge cases.
Automate intake (a staff upload link per clinic) and template the page export.
rebuild.fit: Developers or designers comfortable with cold outreach to local businesses

name: Carrd
tagline: Simple, responsive one-page websites for almost anything
team: Solo founder; AJ (dev/product) plus Doni (operations) as of April 2021
timeToFirstDollar: First $100 came via Twitter from existing HTML5 UP/Pixelarity customers; $1,000 during the Product Hunt launch
summary: Carrd is a builder for single-page websites such as personal profiles, landing pages and link-in-bio pages. It has a free tier and cheap annual Pro plans. AJ, a pseudonymous developer, built it alone, reached $1M ARR with 2.5M sites by April 2021 (with a partial VC round and a two-person team), and told Indie Hackers in 2024 it had reached about $2M ARR with no marketing spend.
origin: AJ was already known for HTML5 UP, a set of free responsive site templates, and its paid sibling Pixelarity, which gave him a Twitter following. Looking for a bigger challenge, he launched Carrd publicly in March 2016 as 'a free platform for building simple, fully responsive one-page sites for pretty much anything'. His first users and first $100 came from Twitter, and his first 1,000 users and $1,000 from Product Hunt.
howItMakesMoney: Freemium, billed annually only: Pro Lite $9/yr, Pro Standard $19/yr and Pro Plus $49/yr. Higher tiers unlock custom domains, forms, embeds and more sites. The very low annual price turns a large free user base into a steady stream of small payments.
growth: Word of mouth and 'Made with Carrd' branding on free sites act as built-in distribution; AJ says growth came entirely from word of mouth.
A signup-free builder flow (you can build a site before creating an account) cut onboarding friction for the Product Hunt launch.
Adopted as an 'extended profile' linked from Twitter and other social platforms, a segment larger site builders ignored.
Seasonal sales (Oct to Dec 2017, Mar 2018) gave clear revenue bumps, which AJ shared in public stats.
Deliberately limited features, keeping the product simple rather than chasing full website-builder parity, with no money spent on marketing.
moat: A very low price anchor ($19/yr) combined with millions of sites and strong brand affinity among young creators makes it hard for competitors to undercut or out-simplify.
risks: Link-in-bio and AI site generators compete for the same simple-site use case. The low price leaves little room if hosting or support costs rise.

timeline.event: Public launch of Carrd
AJ publishes monthly users, sites and revenue stats for Jan 2016 to Apr 2018
Announces 2.5M sites, 1.6M users, $1M ARR and a partly VC-funded round; moves fully to AWS
Indie Hackers interview: Carrd at ~$2M ARR with zero marketing spend

lessons: A tiny annual price can beat monthly SaaS pricing when the free tier is huge and the upgrade is obvious.
Feature restraint is a positioning choice: 'simple one-page' is the product.
An audience from earlier free work (templates) can seed a paid product's launch.
Free-tier branding compounds as a zero-cost acquisition channel.

rebuild.idea: A one-page site builder just for local tradespeople (plumbers, electricians, cleaners) with built-in quote-request forms, service-area maps and Google review embeds, at $29/yr.
rebuild.why: General builders force tradespeople through design choices they don't care about. Most need one page that ranks locally and collects quote requests.
mvp: Build 3 templates with a quote form that emails and texts the owner.
Hand-build 10 sites for tradespeople found through Google Maps listings that have no website.
Charge $29/yr after a 30-day free trial.
Add 'Built with ...' branding to every free site.
rebuild.fit: Front-end developers who can do local outreach
rebuild.pricing: Free branded page on a subdomain, then $29/yr for a custom domain and quote-form SMS alerts, with a $99 done-for-you setup add-on.
rebuild.market: Buyers are owner-operator tradespeople, reached by cold outreach to Google Maps listings without websites, trade Facebook groups and supplier counters. Competitors are Carrd, Wix, Squarespace, GoDaddy's builder and lead platforms like Thumbtack and Angi.

name: Photo AI
tagline: Upload selfies, train a personal AI model, generate realistic photos of yourself
startupCost: <$1k to launch (plus $40k later spent on the photoai.com domain)
summary: Photo AI lets users upload photos of themselves, trains a custom image model on them, and then generates realistic photos in any setting or outfit. Pieter Levels runs it alone. In September 2025 he reported ~$150k/month, 2,573 active subscribers and an 87% profit margin.
origin: Levels launched Avatar AI in 2022, one of the first apps selling AI-generated avatars from selfies. When the avatar fad faded he pivoted the same fine-tuning pipeline into Photo AI in February 2023. The pitch moved from novelty avatars to realistic photos people could use for dating profiles, social media and work.
howItMakesMoney: Monthly subscriptions billed by tier. The public pricing page lists Starter at $19/mo, Pro at $49/mo, Premium at $99/mo and Ultra at $199/mo. Tiers differ mainly in how many models you can train and how many photos you can generate.
growth: Posted MRR, customer counts and costs publicly from week one: $10k MRR after 3 weeks with 318 customers, then $25,337/mo revenue against $5,713/mo costs after 5 weeks.
Went viral on short video: Levels reported adding $7k MRR in one day from a single TikTok (March 2023).
An existing audience of several hundred thousand X followers, built over a decade of public building, gave him launch distribution.
Appeared on the Lex Fridman podcast (Aug 2024). Levels said Photo AI revenue roughly tripled afterwards and posted a $161k/month Photo AI figure in Sept 2024.
Kept upgrading output quality as newer open image models arrived, including ControlNet shortly after launch, and gave the upgrades to paying tiers.
moat: The moat is distribution more than technology. Levels' audience and track record get every launch seen. Fast iteration on new models, plus years of prompt and pipeline tuning, keeps output quality competitive.
risks: Frontier image models from large labs increasingly generate a person's likeness without per-user fine-tuning, which commoditizes the core feature. Revenue depends heavily on one founder's attention, and the market is crowded with clones.

timeline.event: Launches Avatar AI, selling AI avatars generated from selfies
Pivots into Photo AI for realistic AI photos
Reports $10k MRR after 3 weeks, then $18k MRR and buys photoai.com for $40k
Reports $25k MRR after 5 weeks with ~$19.6k/mo profit
Posts $161k/month for Photo AI after appearing on the Lex Fridman podcast
Reports a ~$150k/month record, 2,573 subscribers and 87% margin, still solo

lessons: Reuse the pipeline when a fad dies. Avatar AI's fine-tuning stack became the base for a more durable product.
Public revenue updates double as marketing: each milestone post was also a launch announcement.
Rent GPUs through an inference API (Replicate) instead of running your own ML infrastructure, and keep the web app boring (PHP, SQLite, one VPS).
Put the monthly price up front and tier it by usage. Heavy users self-select into $99 to $199 plans.
Buy the exact-match domain once revenue justifies it. Levels paid $40k, about 2.2 months of MRR at the time.

rebuild.idea: Consistent AI product and lifestyle photos of one physical product (not a person) for small Etsy and Shopify sellers: train on 10 phone photos, then generate catalogue and lifestyle shots on demand.
rebuild.why: Per-subject fine-tuning is now cheap, and small sellers still pay photographers per shoot. Most AI product-photo tools do background swaps, not faithful multi-angle renders of one specific item.
mvp: Build a concierge flow: take 10 photos from a seller, fine-tune an open image model on Replicate, and deliver 40 shots by hand.
Post 3 to 5 before/after sets in Etsy and Shopify seller communities and offer the first 10 sellers a $29 pack.
Automate upload, train, generate and email once 5 people have paid.
Add a $19/mo plan for sellers who add new products every month.
rebuild.fit: Developers comfortable with image-model APIs who can also sell to e-commerce sellers

name: TypingMind
tagline: A better chat interface for LLMs, used with your own API keys
team: Solo until 2025, then founder + 2 hires (1 dev, 1 designer)
summary: TypingMind is a chat front-end for ChatGPT, Claude and other models, where users bring their own API keys. Tony Dinh built it alone in early 2023 and sold one-time licenses, later adding team and cloud plans. In April 2025 he reported $148k revenue for the previous month, an all-time high, and his first two hires.
origin: Dinh, a Vietnamese developer who had already built DevUtils and Black Magic, shipped TypingMind in early March 2023, shortly after OpenAI released the ChatGPT API. He tweeted that he woke up to $428.58 of revenue for the new product. By his own newsletter account it made about $22k in the first 7 days.
howItMakesMoney: One-time licenses for individuals, at $39 (Standard), $79 (Extended) and $99 (Premium) per the current pricing docs. Users pay model providers directly through their own API keys. Subscription offerings include TypingMind Cloud and TypingMind Custom, a white-label chat UI for teams and businesses.
growth: Launched on X to an existing audience of developers, with daily revenue screenshots ($428 on day one, $3,100 soon after).
Rode the ChatGPT API wave: it gave power users a better UI with prompt libraries, plugins and multi-model chat, without a ChatGPT Plus subscription.
Added support for each new model and feature (web search, image generation, artifacts, deep research) quickly after release.
Moved upmarket with TypingMind Custom for teams, which adds recurring B2B revenue on top of one-time licenses.
Ran an affiliate program from 2023.
moat: The moat is speed and polish more than technology: a large installed base of license holders, a plugin ecosystem, and B2B team deployments that are sticky once rolled out.
risks: Model providers keep improving their own chat apps, which shrinks the gap a third-party UI fills. One-time licenses cap lifetime value unless the team and cloud tiers keep growing.

timeline.event: Launches TypingMind and tweets $428.58 of revenue after the first night
Reports ~$22k in the first 7 days
Opens an affiliate program
Reports $148k for the previous month (all-time high) and hires a developer and a designer
Continues adding multi-model, deep research and team features

lessons: When a new platform API ships, the first good UI on top of it can win a big share of early adopters.
Bring-your-own-key pricing removes your biggest variable cost, so a one-time license can be very profitable.
Sell one-time to individuals and recurring to teams, so each segment pays the way it prefers.
Share revenue screenshots early: the first-day numbers were themselves the launch marketing.

rebuild.idea: A bring-your-own-key AI workspace for regulated small firms (law offices, accountants, clinics) that ships with audit logs, PII redaction before prompts leave the machine, and ready-made prompt packs for each profession.
rebuild.why: General chat UIs target individuals and big enterprises. Small regulated firms want to use AI but need redaction and logging they can show to insurers or regulators.
mvp: Fork or build a simple chat UI with a regex and NER PII-redaction layer and a local audit log export.
Write 20 prompts for one profession (e.g. small law firms) with a practitioner.
Offer a $299 one-time license plus a $29/mo 'compliance pack' to 20 firms reached through LinkedIn and local bar associations.
Collect testimonials and publish a one-page compliance explainer.
rebuild.fit: Full-stack developers with a contact inside a regulated profession

name: Remote OK
tagline: Remote job board that started as an aggregator of remote listings
summary: Remote OK is one of the largest remote-only job boards. Pieter Levels built it in 2015 by aggregating remote jobs from other boards, then turned it into a paid job-posting board. It is famous for running on a single PHP file. It peaked at $101,101 in one month in April 2021. Later in 2024 Levels said remote work had fallen to 23% of his total revenue.
origin: Levels built it as a daily aggregator that pulled remote listings from non-remote job boards. It later merged with his Nomad Jobs board to become a standalone job board, and it launched to #1 on Product Hunt. Traffic from the aggregated listings is what made companies willing to pay to post directly.
howItMakesMoney: Employers pay per job post, advertised as 'from $299 for 30 days' with bundles, and add-ons such as highlighting and pinning. Levels frequently tests prices dynamically. In April 2021 revenue was about $92K from job posts plus about $9.5K from ads.
growth: Aggregating listings solved the chicken-and-egg problem. The board had thousands of jobs, and therefore job seekers, before any employer paid.
Building in public on X and his blog: revenue screenshots and 'single PHP file' posts spread widely.
SEO from programmatic pages per role, tag and location (e.g. 'remote Python jobs').
Remote hiring spiked in 2020-2021, and the board was already the obvious destination.
moat: Brand and domain authority built up over a decade, plus a large base of job seekers that employers pay to reach. Neither can be copied quickly.
risks: Highly cyclical, since revenue follows remote hiring demand, which cooled after 2021. There are many free competing boards and aggregators, and Google for Jobs sits in front of job boards in search results.

timeline.event: Launches as a remote job aggregator; reaches #1 on Product Hunt
Nomad List and Remote OK together pass $1M annual revenue after 4 years
Single index.php earns $101,101 in a month
Levels says remote work is now 23% of his revenue, with AI products at 62%

lessons: Seed a marketplace by aggregating existing supply before asking anyone to pay.
Boring tech is fine. A single PHP file handled six-figure months.
Keep testing prices on job posts. Employers are much less price-sensitive than job seekers.
A niche job board follows its labor market. Plan for the cycle turning.

rebuild.idea: A job board for data engineering and analytics engineering roles, aggregated from public ATS feeds (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby), with normalized stack tags (dbt, Airflow, Spark, Snowflake) and salary filters.
rebuild.why: Generic boards tag jobs poorly by data stack, and many ATS systems expose public JSON job feeds. A data engineer can build a much better-structured index than a general board.
mvp: Pull ~2,000 companies' public ATS endpoints nightly and classify postings with keyword rules plus an LLM pass for stack and seniority
Publish programmatic pages per tool+location (e.g. 'remote dbt jobs')
Launch a free weekly email digest to build the job-seeker audience
Charge $199 for a featured post and offer the first 5 free to data-tool startups in exchange for posting
rebuild.fit: A data engineer who knows the stack vocabulary and can build a reliable nightly ETL

name: Bannerbear
tagline: API for auto-generating images and videos from templates
team: Solo founder until about $10k MRR (first contractor, a freelance writer, hired May 2021); now founder plus a small team
timeToFirstDollar: About 9 months with $0 from his 12-startups challenge (Jan to Aug 2019); Previewmojo then reached about $400 MRR by the end of 2019
summary: Bannerbear is an API and no-code tool that generates social images, banners, PDFs and videos from templates. Marketing teams and developers use it to produce creative assets at scale. Jon Yongfook bootstrapped it in public from 2019 and announced $1M ARR in September 2025, built on Rails 6 and jQuery.
origin: Yongfook left his job in January 2019 with about two years of savings. He spent most of that year on a '12 startups in 12 months' challenge, launching 7 products that earned no direct revenue. One of them, Previewmojo (launched November 2019), auto-generated open-graph preview images and reached about $400 MRR. Users kept asking for other image sizes, so he widened it and relaunched it as Bannerbear in January 2020, then as a REST API in March 2020.
howItMakesMoney: Monthly subscriptions based on API credits: the pricing page lists Automate at $49/mo (1,000 API credits), Scale from $149/mo (10,000+ credits) and Enterprise from $299/mo (50,000+ credits), with a free trial of 30 credits. Early on Yongfook wrote a post titled 'Don't Charge $9 a Month for Your SaaS'.
growth: Pivoted from a narrow OG-image tool to a general image and video API, which widened the market beyond one small use case.
Integration-led distribution: Zapier, Airtable, Make and WordPress integrations put it in front of no-code users alongside API developers.
Documentation and tutorials: Yongfook found that the more documentation he wrote, the more conversions he got, and hired a freelance writer for tutorial content in 2021.
A 50% coding / 50% marketing rhythm (a week of shipping, then a week of tweeting and blogging about it) plus open-startup milestone posts.
Repositioned around two jobs to be done, 'automate' and 'scale' your marketing, and priced for businesses ($49+ entry tier) instead of cheap consumer plans.
moat: Template tooling, integration listings and accumulated SEO content create switching costs and discovery advantages. Once customers wire the API into their workflows they rarely move.
risks: Cheaper alternatives and generative AI image tools compete on price. Growth took years and depends on continued SEO and integration-directory visibility.

timeline.event: Quits his job and starts 12 startups in 12 months
Launches Previewmojo (auto OG images), reaching about $400 MRR by the end of the year
Rebrands and pivots to Bannerbear, auto-generating banners in many sizes
Launches the Bannerbear REST API and template editor; pulls out of the Shopify app store
Passes $10k MRR ($10,455), documented in 'Journey to $10k MRR'
Publishes '7 Lessons Growing a Bootstrapped SaaS to $50K MRR'
Announces $1M ARR, built on Rails 6 and jQuery

lessons: Ship many small experiments, then widen the one that gets paying users.
APIs with no-code integrations reach both developers and operators, so ship integrations early.
Charge B2B prices from day one. $9/mo plans attract the wrong customers.
Boring tech (Rails, jQuery) is enough to reach $1M ARR. Spend effort on distribution instead.

rebuild.idea: A template-to-PDF and image API for real-estate agents' listing flyers and social posts, pulling data straight from MLS/IDX feeds.
rebuild.why: General image APIs need a developer to wire them up. Agents and brokerages want flyers generated automatically whenever a listing changes.
mvp: Build 5 flyer and social templates and a script that fills them from one brokerage's IDX feed.

name: Photopea
tagline: Free browser-based image editor that opens Photoshop files, funded by ads
summary: Photopea is a free web image editor built by Ukrainian developer Ivan Kutskir that opens PSD and other formats in the browser. howItMakesMoney: Display ads to free users, a paid Premium option that removes ads (listed at about $5/month), and licensing deals with other companies.
growth: Solved a specific need: opening and editing PSD files for free without installing Photoshop
Posted in Photoshop-related subreddits and ran Reddit AMAs (e.g. 2018)
Kept the product free, so users shared it in schools and design communities
Ad revenue reportedly doubled roughly every six months after 2017
Very low running costs (hosting in the hundreds of dollars per year) let almost all revenue be profit
moat: Years of solo work on file-format compatibility (PSD, XCF, Sketch and more) that is hard to replicate, plus strong search presence as the free Photoshop alternative.
risks: Heavy reliance on ad networks and search traffic; Adobe's own web and free tiers or AI image tools could erode usage.

Releases Photopea
Adds ads at ~5,000 daily users; ~$500/month at first
Reddit AMA brings a wave of new users
Earns ~$500K for the year (per interview)

Ads work when usage is large and sessions are long
Long pre-revenue periods are survivable when costs are near zero
Doing all the code yourself can make maintenance and fixes faster

name: Nomad List (now Nomads.com)
tagline: City data and a paid community for remote workers choosing where to live
summary: Nomad List ranks cities for remote workers on cost of living, internet speed, weather and safety, and sells membership to a community of nomads. Pieter Levels started it in 2014 as a crowdsourced spreadsheet and has run it mostly alone ever since. It was rebranded to Nomads.com in 2024.
origin: In 2014 Levels was running out of money and set himself a challenge to launch 12 startups in 12 months. He tweeted a public Google Spreadsheet asking people to add data on cities good for remote work, and it filled up quickly. He then turned the sheet into a website, which became Nomad List.
howItMakesMoney: Paid membership unlocks the community (chat, meetups, dating and member features) and full city data. The membership price and billing model have changed many times; exact current prices aren't included here because none could be confirmed from a primary source. Sponsorships and ads have also contributed.
growth: The crowdsourced spreadsheet validated demand before any code was written, and contributors became the first audience.
SEO: thousands of city and comparison pages ('cost of living in X') bring in steady organic search traffic.
Open-startup transparency: Levels published live revenue and user dashboards from 2018, which fed press coverage and his own following.
Conversion experiments: he reported sign-ups up 26% after adding Stripe Checkout and ran randomized tests of the benefits shown in the sign-up modal.
Combined with Remote OK, he reported $83,333+/mo (a $1M/yr run rate) in May 2019 with 0 ad budget and 0 funding.
moat: More than a decade of crowdsourced city data and reviews, strong SEO rankings, and a paid community with network effects are hard to replicate quickly.
risks: Revenue swings with travel trends (COVID hit it hard) and with the remote-work cycle. The product depends on one founder who now spreads his attention across many projects.

timeline.event: Tweets a crowdsourced Google Sheet of nomad-friendly cities during the 12 startups in 12 months challenge, then launches the site
Becomes an Open Startup with public revenue and user stats
Nomad List + Remote OK pass $83,333/mo ($1M/yr run rate) with 1 VPS and no funding
Levels reports ~$700k/yr across his one-person business, mostly Nomad List and Remote OK
Rebrands to Nomads.com
Reports ~$61k/month from Nomad List in a record portfolio month

lessons: Validate with a spreadsheet before writing code: a public sheet can prove demand in a day.
Programmatic data pages (one per city, one per comparison) compound SEO for years.
Monetize the community, not just the data. Public data brings people in and membership pays the bills.
Keep infrastructure tiny. Levels reported running both sites from 1 VPS at ~$5.5k/mo total costs in 2019.

rebuild.idea: A 'where to live' data site plus paid community for remote-working families: school options, pediatric care, kid-friendly neighborhoods and visa rules for dependents, city by city.
rebuild.why: Nomad-focused sites are built around single travellers. Families relocating for remote work have different, higher-stakes data needs and are willing to pay more.
mvp: Start a public Google Sheet of 30 cities with columns for international schools, fees and pediatric hospitals, and post it in remote-family Facebook groups and subreddits.
Interview 10 families who moved abroad and write 5 in-depth city guides from those interviews.
Ship a static site from the sheet with one page per city.
Sell a $49/year membership that includes a private chat and monthly city deep-dive calls.
rebuild.fit: Parents who have relocated abroad and can seed the community from lived experience

name: GummySearch
tagline: Audience research tool that mined Reddit for pain points and buying intent
summary: GummySearch let founders and marketers search Reddit communities for pain points, solution requests and buying intent. Its solo founder, Fed, grew it to about 135,000 registered users, roughly 10,000 paying customers, and about $35K MRR. It shut down in November 2025 after failing to get a commercial license for Reddit's Data API. It is a clear example of platform risk for data businesses.
origin: Fed first built The Hive Index, a directory of online communities, as a warm-up project after going indie. To promote it on Reddit he wrote scripts to find relevant conversations. That internal tool became GummySearch in 2021.
howItMakesMoney: Monthly subscriptions. Reported tiers were Free, Starter $29/mo, Pro $59/mo and Mega $199/mo. Early on, a private lifetime deal priced at 10x the monthly plan raised about $50K from 234 customers.
growth: The audience was indie hackers who live on Reddit and X, and Fed built in public for that same audience.
The lifetime deal funded early development: about $50K in roughly two months.
Word of mouth from recommendations. One tweet in Jan 2024 brought 10 customers and $580 MRR, which had previously taken a year.
Its use as a 'find your customers' research tool made it a common recommendation in founder communities.
moat: A polished UX and categorization layer (pain points, solution requests, themes) on top of Reddit data, plus a strong brand among indie founders. It turned out to have no moat against the data source itself.
risks: This risk ended the business. Reddit's 2023 API pricing and data-usage policy meant a commercial license was required, and a solo, non-VC business couldn't reach an agreement. The product closed to new business on November 30, 2025.

timeline.event: Launches as a spin-out of Fed's Reddit scripts for The Hive Index
Private lifetime deal raises ~$50K from 234 customers
Reddit introduces paid commercial API access
About $3K MRR (Indie Hackers post)
Announces shutdown at ~$35K MRR, ~10,000 paying customers and 135,000 users; stops new sales Nov 30

lessons: If your product is a layer on top of someone else's data, get a license (or a second source) before you get big enough to be noticed.
Internal scripts you wrote for your own marketing can become the product.
A 10x-monthly lifetime deal to early fans can fund a solo build without investors.
Sell insights (pain points, intent), not raw search. That is what people paid $29-199/mo for.

rebuild.idea: A customer-research tool built on licensed or first-party sources: public app-store reviews, G2/Capterra-style reviews the customer exports, support tickets and sales call transcripts, clustered into pain points and feature requests.
rebuild.why: GummySearch's shutdown left users looking for alternatives, and the lesson is to avoid data you can't license. Customers' own exported data, plus sources with stable public access, avoid the same fate.
mvp: Build ingestion for 3 sources: app store reviews, CSV exports from a review platform, and Intercom/Zendesk ticket exports
Cluster into themes with embeddings and show quotes with counts and trends
Offer a free 'analyze your app's reviews' report as a lead magnet
Charge $49/mo and sell to 10 indie SaaS or mobile app founders from GummySearch-alternative threads
rebuild.fit: A data engineer comfortable with ETL from many small sources, embeddings and clustering

A lifetime-fee community can still be sold if membership and content are documented

name: ScreenshotOne
tagline: Screenshot API: send a URL or HTML, get back a clean rendered image
timeToFirstDollar: About 2 months (launched May 2022; first $7 MRR in July 2022)
summary: A developer API that renders any URL, HTML or Markdown into a screenshot, with ad and cookie-banner blocking, full-page capture and video. Dmytro Krasun launched it solo in May 2022 after leaving a server-side engineering job. He grew it to about 1,000 customers and ~$32K MRR, then growth went flat. He publicly analyzed that plateau with Jason Cohen.
origin: Krasun, a backend engineer, left his job and chose a market where people already paid to solve the problem: rendering web pages to images. He launched on May 29, 2022, got his first customer at $7/mo in July 2022, and kept shipping features based on customer requests.
howItMakesMoney: Tiered monthly plans by screenshot volume. Reported plans: free (100 screenshots/mo), Basic $17/mo (2,000), Growth $79/mo (10,000), Scale $259/mo (50,000), with per-screenshot overage and two months free on annual billing.
growth: Search intent. Coverage reports that most new customers come from high-intent Google queries like 'screenshot API'.
Free utilities and open documentation earned backlinks that lift the paid API's search ranking.
Many small integrations and SDKs, and later a CLI and an MCP server, made it easy to adopt from different stacks.
Steady public reporting of milestones ($10K, $20K, $32K MRR) on X and WIP kept the product visible to indie developers.
moat: A reliable product that renders pages at scale, handles banners, lazy loading and anti-bot quirks, and has earned years of search ranking. It is a boring, hard-to-get-right product, not one with deep defensibility.
risks: The market has a ceiling. On the Jason Cohen call, the numbers showed ~9% monthly churn capping MRR near $40K, and no single large, repeatable buyer segment had appeared. Cheap competitors and self-hosted Playwright/Puppeteer also put pressure on price.

timeline.event: ScreenshotOne launches
First paying customer at $7/mo
Crosses ~$14K MRR (Morning Maker Show interview)
Reaches ~$20K MRR
Around $32K MRR with ~1,000 customers and flat growth; reviews the plateau live with Jason Cohen

lessons: Pick a boring category where people already pay. It removes demand risk, and an existing category makes SEO easy.
Churn sets a ceiling: max MRR is roughly new MRR per month divided by the churn rate. Measure it before you plan to 3x.
Free tools and good documentation work as the marketing for an API business.
A usage-based API with small plans brings many small customers. Growing past a plateau usually takes a new buyer segment, not more of the same traffic.

rebuild.idea: A compliance evidence capture API that takes timestamped, hashed and archived captures of web pages (ads, pricing pages, cookie banners, terms) for legal, ad-compliance and brand-protection teams.
rebuild.why: General screenshot APIs compete on price. Regulated buyers such as ad compliance, consumer-protection disputes and affiliate monitoring pay for tamper-evident chain of custody, which generic tools don't offer.
mvp: Wrap Playwright captures with SHA-256 hashing, RFC 3161 timestamping and WARC export
Add scheduled captures across geographies/proxies with a diff view
Interview 10 affiliate-compliance or brand-protection managers and pre-sell a $99-299/mo plan
Ship a one-page 'evidence report' PDF, since that is the artifact buyers forward to lawyers
rebuild.fit: A backend or data engineer who likes infrastructure and can sell to non-technical compliance teams

tagline: Embeddable store locator that shows shoppers where to buy a brand's products
team: Solo founder for most of its life; a small part-time team near the 2017 sale
summary: Storemapper is a store locator widget for brands that sell through retailers. It embeds on Shopify, BigCommerce, WordPress, Squarespace and other sites. Tyler Tringas taught himself to code, built the first version on a long flight, grew it while traveling, and sold it to SureSwift Capital in July 2017. It is the case he later used to coin the term 'micro-SaaS'.
origin: Tringas spent about nine months learning to code, then built Storemapper's first version on a single long flight to Argentina. He charged $5/mo because the first version was buggy, and had paying customers within about 24 hours.
howItMakesMoney: Monthly subscriptions. It started at $5/mo, and he raised the price 80% to $9/mo for new customers once the product matured, then raised it further in later years. The early low price is his own documented lesson in underpricing.
growth: Platform app stores. Listing on Shopify's app store and building integrations for BigCommerce, WordPress and Squarespace put it in front of merchants on fast-growing platforms.
A viral footer. The 'powered by Storemapper' link on nearly every customer's locator produced thousands of clicks a month.
Organic search for 'store locator' terms. He never ran paid ads.
Repeated price increases on new customers raised ARPU without adding more customers.
moat: A small but real set of integrations across ecommerce platforms and embedded widgets that are annoying to replace. The niche was too small for large companies to target.
risks: Platform dependence: Shopify can ship a native locator or change app-store rules. Competing plugins are cheap, and a low-ARPU product with churn needs constant new customers.

timeline.event: Builds the first version on a flight to Argentina and gets paying customers within about a day at $5/mo
Publishes 'bootstrapped to $50,000/year in 2 years' with live metrics
Publishes '2015 Roadmap: 100K to 4HWW' about getting to $100K ARR on a four-hour week
Indie Hackers interview: ~$21K/mo, driven by targeting the right niche
Indie Hackers podcast: ~$25K/mo
Sold to SureSwift Capital for an undisclosed 'level up money' price after meeting buyers at MicroConf

lessons: Build on top of a fast-growing platform's app store. Its growth becomes your distribution.
Ship embedded products with a 'powered by' link so every customer markets for you.
Don't anchor on your launch price. Raise it for new customers once the product works.
A narrow utility can support a traveling solo founder and still be sellable to a SaaS holding company.

rebuild.why: Generic store locators assume the brand keeps a clean store list. Beverage and food brands selling through distributors get irregular spreadsheets, so their 'where to buy' pages go stale.

Ship an embeddable map widget with Shopify and WordPress snippets
Charge $29/mo with a monthly 'upload your report' email and auto-refresh
Sell directly to 20 local breweries via Instagram DMs and state brewers' guild forums

name: Easlo
tagline: Notion templates for students and solo workers, sold on Gumroad

timeToFirstDollar: Tips on free templates from summer/fall 2021; first paid template (Nov 2021) made over $3,000 in its first month
summary: Easlo is the brand of Jason Chin, a Singaporean creator who sells Notion templates such as the Second Brain system. He reported $239K in template sales in 2022 as a one-person operation (Business Insider verified the figure), and by 2024 had tens of thousands of customers and 1.1M+ followers across platforms.
origin: Chin learned Notion from YouTube videos on weekends while doing national service in Singapore. In summer 2021 he released free templates (such as budget and habit trackers) on Gumroad with an optional tip and promoted them on Twitter and Product Hunt. After receiving tips of up to $100, he began charging for new templates in November 2021, and chose to go full time as a creator instead of attending university.
howItMakesMoney: One-time purchases of Notion templates on Gumroad, typically $10-$100. In 2022 the flagship Second Brain template sold at $130 and brought in over $100K on its own, while cheaper templates such as a $20 Bullet Journal and $40 Finance Tracker made up nearly half the business. Second Brain is listed at $79 on Gumroad today.
growth: Released templates free with an optional tip first, then emailed everyone who had downloaded them when he started charging
Started with simple personal-organization templates (budget, habits) aimed at people like himself
Grew organically on Twitter (over 211K followers by late 2022) with 2-3 tweets a day and a weekly thread, never paying for ads, then repeated the playbook on TikTok and Instagram
Launched templates on Product Hunt and priced an all-in-one Second Brain system well above single-purpose templates
moat: Weak on the product (templates are easy to copy) but strong on distribution: a large social following and brand recognition in the Notion template niche.
risks: Depends on Notion's popularity and on Notion's own template marketplace; AI tools that generate workspaces could commoditize templates.

name: Pinboard
tagline: Paid, ad-free bookmarking with optional full-page archiving
timeToFirstDollar: At launch (paid signup fee from day one)
summary: Pinboard is a bookmarking site launched in July 2009 and run by Maciej Ceglowski. It has charged users from the start and has no ads. He published yearly revenue of $117K-$234K for 2010-2016 against running costs of about $17K a year.
origin: Ceglowski built Pinboard as a faster, simpler alternative to Delicious. At launch it charged a one-time signup fee of a few dollars that rose by a fraction of a cent with each new user, to slow growth and deter spam. Months later he added a $25/year archiving option, and it became his full-time job at around 1,200 users.
howItMakesMoney: Annual subscriptions: a standard account (listed at $22/year in recent years) and an archiving account (listed at $39/year) that saves copies of bookmarked pages. It moved from one-time fees to annual subscriptions in 2015.
growth: Absorbed users each time Delicious had trouble (Yahoo's 2010 plans to sunset it caused a large influx)
Charging from day one filtered for committed users and kept spam down
A plain, fast interface appealed to heavy readers and developers who recommended it
Ceglowski's writing and talks on the web and privacy kept Pinboard visible
moat: Years of users' bookmark and archive data plus trust in a privacy-respecting, ad-free service; switching means migrating a personal library.
risks: Single-maintainer bus factor and slow feature development; browser read-later and AI note tools compete for the same use.

timeline.event: Launches with a rising one-time signup fee
Adds $25/year archiving accounts; becomes full-time at ~1,200 users
Delicious shutdown news drives a surge of signups; revenue $117K for the year
Moves to annual subscriptions; revenue dips then recovers
Publishes revenue of $234K for the year and ~$17K annual running costs
Buys Delicious for $35,000

lessons: Charging from day one limits growth but gives a profitable, low-support user base
A competitor's decline can be the main growth channel if you are the obvious alternative
Keeping infrastructure simple keeps costs a small fraction of revenue
Recurring annual billing smooths revenue compared with one-time fees

rebuild.idea: A paid, private archive for a specific profession's web sources, such as lawyers or journalists capturing web pages as timestamped evidence
rebuild.why: Web pages change or disappear often, and professionals who must prove what a page said have few simple, low-cost tools outside expensive enterprise suites.
mvp: Build a browser extension that saves a page snapshot with a timestamp and hash
Give it to 10 journalists or paralegals for feedback
Charge $5-10/month from the first paying user with a simple export feature
Write one article on citing archived pages and share it in professional forums
rebuild.fit: A web developer with contacts in journalism or legal work

name: ShipFast
tagline: Next.js boilerplate with auth, payments and email pre-wired for SaaS launches
summary: ShipFast is a paid Next.js starter codebase with authentication, Stripe payments, database, emails and SEO pages already wired up. Marc Lou built it in about a week in 2023 from code he had reused across his own projects. He reported $384k in its first 7 months and $1M+ lifetime, with monthly sales declining since the 2024 peak.
origin: Lou, a French developer who had been shipping many small startups in public, packaged the code he kept rewriting for each new project. He launched it around Aug 31/Sept 1 2023 with '$50 off for the first 50 customers', and told his wife they'd be lucky to make $100.
howItMakesMoney: One-time purchase for lifetime access to the GitHub repo and updates. Tiers have ranged from about $169 to $299 depending on whether they include a private Discord community and his CodeFast course. It also works as the entry product in Lou's portfolio (CodeFast, DataFast, TrustMRR).
growth: Built in public on X with frequent revenue posts to a fast-growing indie-hacker audience.
Leaderboards and 'customers who shipped with ShipFast' posts turned buyers into promoters. He reported 4,000 developers by July 2024 and 5,000+ by Nov 2024.
Named Product Hunt Maker of the Year 2023, which added credibility and backlinks.
Tested paid ads: he reported $8,345 in Facebook ads bringing in $23,283 of ShipFast revenue (April 2024).
Cross-sold into his other products (CodeFast course, DataFast analytics) to offset ShipFast's decline.
moat: Weak on the code itself, since boilerplates are easy to copy and many clones exist. The defensibility is Lou's audience, the community Discord and brand recognition among indie hackers.
risks: AI coding tools now generate boilerplate on demand, which undercuts the core value, and ShipFast's monthly sales have fallen well below the 2024 peak. Revenue depends on the founder's personal reach.

timeline.event: Launches ShipFast with $50 off for the first 50 customers
Named Product Hunt Maker of the Year 2023
Reports $384k in the first 7 months
Reports 5,000+ builders have used ShipFast
ShipFast makes $18.2k of Lou's $48.9k monthly total
ShipFast makes $17.2k; TrustMRR has overtaken it as his top product

lessons: Package the code you already reuse. The fastest product to build is one you have effectively written several times.
A one-time developer product can spike quickly on an audience but decays without new distribution.
Use a successful product as a funnel into newer products (courses, SaaS) before it plateaus.
Share exact ad-spend numbers: the Facebook ads result was itself a viral post.

rebuild.why: Generic SaaS boilerplates cover auth and Stripe but not LLM cost metering, tenant isolation or evals, which every B2B AI app now has to rebuild.
mvp: Extract the metering, billing and audit pieces from an AI app you've already built into a clean repo.
Write a public post comparing the cost of building them from scratch with using the kit.
Pre-sell at $149 to your network and on X or relevant Discords before polishing.
Record a 20-minute walkthrough video as the main sales asset.
rebuild.fit: Engineers who have shipped a B2B AI product and have some audience on X or GitHub

name: BetaList
tagline: Directory of early-stage startups looking for their first users
team: Solo founder; daily operations later delegated to a collaborator (@rpish)
summary: BetaList features pre-launch and newly launched startups to an audience of early adopters. Marc Köhlbrugge started it in December 2010 on Tumblr. After 10 years it had featured 15,000+ startups, reviewed 70,000+ submissions, welcomed 100,000+ registered users and made almost $1M in total revenue. It makes money from advertising and sponsorships and by charging founders to skip the free review queue.
origin: In late 2010 Köhlbrugge and friends were building Openmargin, an iPad app, and struggling to get beta sign-ups. Over a weekend he built BetaLi.st, a modified Tumblr theme collecting 'coming soon' pages, and pitched it to TechCrunch, hoping to redirect the coverage to his own app. TechCrunch wrote about it in December 2010. He didn't plan to monetize it until companies started asking how to get featured.
howItMakesMoney: (1) Advertising: he started paid slots at $50/week and kept doubling the price until buyers said no, reaching $1,500/week by 2020. The advertise page now lists a $4,999/month sponsorship and self-serve 'Boost' placements at $99/week or $199/month. (2) Expedited review: he first let founders skip the queue for free as a favor, then charged $15, and kept raising it to $199 by 2020.
growth: A free submission queue with a paid fast lane. The backlog itself creates demand for the paid option.
Early press: a December 2010 TechCrunch article, and later Marc's 2014 post 'How I tricked TechCrunch into writing about my startup', which he says drove even more visits than the original article.
Each featured startup shares its listing, which brings in more founders and early-adopter subscribers.
He kept testing prices on ad slots and expedited reviews, raising them until demand dropped.
moat: More than a decade of brand recognition in the startup-launch niche, an email and user base of early adopters, and domain authority that makes a listing worth paying for.
risks: Launch directories are easy to start and there are hundreds now. Product Hunt dominates attention, and a directory's value falls if its audience stops engaging.

timeline.event: BetaList (then BetaLi.st) launches as a Tumblr site and is covered by TechCrunch
Marc publishes 'How I tricked TechCrunch into writing about my startup'
10-year recap: 15,000+ startups featured, 70,000+ submissions reviewed, 100,000+ users, almost $1M total revenue; ads at $1,500/week and expedited review at $199

lessons: A free queue plus a paid skip-the-line option is a simple, scalable way for a directory to make money.
Price ads by doubling until customers say no. His started at $50/week and reached $1,500/week.
Start with no-code (a Tumblr theme) and rebuild only after demand shows up.
Delegating daily operations freed him to start other products (WIP, startup.jobs) while BetaList kept earning.

rebuild.idea: A curated directory of MCP servers and AI-agent tools with verified install and compatibility testing, a free listing queue and a paid expedited review with a badge.
rebuild.why: The number of agent tools and MCP servers is growing fast, and discovery is fragmented across GitHub and X. Builders will pay for fast review and a trustworthy 'tested' badge.

Run each through a scripted install test and publish pass/fail
Add a free submit form with a 3-4 week queue and a $49 'review in 48h' option via Stripe
Post the weekly 'new tools' list on X and in AI builder communities to grow the audience
rebuild.fit: An engineer who can automate scraping and testing pipelines and enjoys curation
rebuild.pricing: Free listings with a slow queue, a $49 one-time expedited review with a 'tested' badge, and $99/week featured placements once the newsletter has a few thousand subscribers.
rebuild.market: Buyers are developers and small AI-tool startups who want users; reach them through X, Hacker News, Reddit and a weekly newsletter. Competitors include Smithery, mcp.so, Glama's MCP directory, the official MCP registry and general launch sites like Product Hunt.

name: Bingo Card Creator
tagline: Software that makes printable bingo cards for elementary school teachers

revenue.label: $64.8K sales in 2012 (~$38.6K profit), its best year

stack: A/Bingo (his own Rails A/B testing library)
summary: Patrick McKenzie (patio11) built a narrow tool for teachers who make bingo cards and published its sales, profit and marketing experiments every year. He started it in 2006 while working as a salaryman in Japan. It grew into a profitable, mostly automated side business that peaked at about $65K in sales in 2012, and he sold it through FE International in 2015.
origin: McKenzie released Bingo Card Creator 1.0 on July 1, 2006 as a downloadable Java app, after about 47 hours of work. Teachers made bingo cards for vocabulary and lessons by hand, and he automated that job. From 2009 it ran almost entirely as a Rails web app, which let him A/B test the funnel.
howItMakesMoney: A one-time purchase (raised from $24.95 to $29.95 in 2009) after a free trial, with sales from elementary school teachers and strong seasonal spikes around holidays. Historically it ran at about a 60% profit margin.
growth: Long-tail SEO. He made one landing page per narrow topic (specific holiday or vocabulary bingo cards), later written by freelancers at scale. He says that content grew to about 50% of sales and 75% of profits.
Conversion optimization. He wrote A/Bingo, an open-source Rails A/B testing library, and tested copy, landing pages and the purchase flow.
A 2012 redesign and Stripe card payments lifted trial-to-purchase conversion from 1.8% to 2.4%. He called them the best thing that happened to the business in years.
The business ran in maintenance mode about 48 weeks a year, so his time went into marketing systems rather than features.
moat: Years of accumulated long-tail pages and search rankings in a niche too small for bigger companies to target. The product itself is easy to copy. The distribution is not.
risks: Google algorithm changes, and free alternatives or template sites. The seasonal teacher market has limited room to grow; sales were roughly flat in 2011, and he eventually sold mainly to focus on his other businesses.

timeline.event: Bingo Card Creator 1.0 launches as downloadable software
Web version launches; price raised from $24.95 to $29.95
Passes $50,000 in lifetime sales; releases A/Bingo split-testing library
Quits his Japanese salaryman job to run his software business full time
BCC sales roughly flat at $45.5K (about $22.9K profit) while consulting grows
Redesign and Stripe checkout lift conversion; best year ever at $64.8K sales and $38.6K profit
Sold through FE International, about five months from start to close

lessons: Pick a narrow, unglamorous job for a specific user (teachers making bingo cards) where competition is weak.
Programmatic long-tail content, one page per micro-query, can outperform head-term SEO for small products.
Instrument everything and A/B test the funnel. Checkout and payment changes can matter more than features.
Publish your numbers every year. The transparency built him an audience that later paid for consulting and courses.

rebuild.idea: A generator for printable, standards-aligned classroom activities (word searches, bingo, flashcards) that takes a teacher's own vocabulary list and aligns to phonics or ESL curricula, sold to homeschoolers and ESL tutors.
rebuild.why: Generic worksheet sites don't map to specific curricula or learner levels. LLMs now make it cheap to produce structured, level-appropriate content from a list, but it needs a strict template layer to print well.
mvp: Pick one curriculum (e.g. a popular phonics sequence or CEFR A1-A2 ESL) and build the generator for it
Programmatically publish 200 free landing pages, one per lesson or word list, each with a sample PDF
Put printing behind a $5/mo or $39/yr plan and post in 3 homeschool or ESL tutor communities
A/B test the paywall copy and checkout from day one
rebuild.fit: An engineer who can do programmatic SEO and PDF templating and knows (or can interview) teachers
rebuild.pricing: Freemium generator with watermark-free printing on a $5/mo or $39/yr plan, plus a $99/yr multi-student license for tutors and co-ops.
rebuild.market: Buyers are homeschooling parents and independent ESL/phonics tutors, reached through programmatic SEO pages, Pinterest, homeschool Facebook groups and tutor communities. Competitors are Teachers Pay Teachers, Twinkl, Education.com and free generators like Canva and Wordwall.

name: Better Sheets
tagline: Library of Google Sheets tutorials, templates and Apps Script tools
summary: Better Sheets sells a membership to hundreds of screencast tutorials, templates and small tools that help people get more out of Google Sheets. Andrew Kamphey launched it after a 24-hour sprint in April 2020, passed $100K in top-line revenue after two years and $200K by its third anniversary, mostly from lifetime-access sales on AppSumo. By mid-2024 Indie Hackers profiled it as a ~$5K/month lifestyle business.
origin: Kamphey spent about five years as the 'Google Sheets guy' at an entertainment startup, automating work with Apps Script, then went out on his own in 2018. After other products stalled, he launched Better Sheets on April 3, 2020 as a 24-hour project: 8 screencast videos, 4 free and 4 behind a paywall. It made $390 from 13 sales in April 2020 and $2,291 from 134 sales in May 2020, and he kept recording tutorials based on what members asked for.
howItMakesMoney: Mostly lifetime memberships. Lifetime access was $19 for the first year or so, then $49, $69 by May 2022, $225 in late 2023 and $250 from February 2024; a monthly plan was added around 2022-23. In his two-year breakdown, lifetime memberships were about 80% of revenue and AppSumo about 85% of sales. By 2024 revenue also came from Gumroad templates, subscriptions and consulting via Stripe, Udemy courses and YouTube ads.
growth: AppSumo's marketplace put the lifetime deal in front of a large audience of buyers already looking for tools, and did much of the marketing in exchange for its cut.
Answering members' requests with new tutorials kept growing the library, which justified raising the lifetime price step by step.
A free template pack for AppSumo users (34,000 downloads by May 2022), a Product Hunt launch that reached #1 Product of the Day in 2022, and milestone posts on Indie Hackers.
Later diversified into Google Sheets add-ons, small one-page tools, Udemy courses and YouTube to smooth out lumpy lifetime-deal revenue.
moat: A large back catalog of focused Sheets tutorials and templates plus a recognizable personal brand ('the Sheets guy'). The content can be copied piece by piece, but the full library and audience are harder to copy.
risks: Lifetime pricing makes revenue spiky and front-loaded, with no recurring base. AI assistants inside Google Sheets (Gemini) can answer many 'how do I' questions for free.

timeline.event: Launched after a 24-hour sprint; 13 sales / $390 in the first month
134 sales / $2,291 in the second month
Passes $100K in top-line revenue in two years; relaunches the site on Rails and hits #1 Product of the Day on Product Hunt
Third anniversary: $200K total revenue
Indie Hackers profiles Better Sheets as a ~$5K/month lifestyle business

lessons: Teaching a ubiquitous tool (Sheets) to a narrow audience can be a business on its own.
Lifetime deals raise cash fast but are not recurring revenue. Keep track of which one you are building.
Let members' questions set the content roadmap. Each answered question becomes a new tutorial.
Ship in 24 hours, then raise prices as the library grows.

rebuild.idea: A library of Google Sheets and Apps Script automations and tutorials for small bookkeeping and accounting practices, such as bank CSV cleanup, client reconciliation trackers and AI-assisted categorization scripts.
rebuild.why: General Sheets tutorials now compete with built-in AI help. Workflow packs for one profession, bundled with working scripts, still save hours and are easy to pay for.
mvp: Interview 10 solo bookkeepers about their most repeated spreadsheet chore
Build 5 working template+script bundles and a short screencast for each
Sell a $99/yr membership (plus a lifetime launch price) through bookkeeper Facebook groups and Reddit
Publish one free tutorial per week for SEO and YouTube
rebuild.fit: Someone with data-processing and spreadsheet skills who can record clear screencasts
rebuild.pricing: A $99/yr membership for the full bundle library, with a limited $199 lifetime launch deal and $29-$49 single bundles on Gumroad.
rebuild.market: Buyers are solo bookkeepers and small accounting practices, reached through bookkeeper Facebook groups, r/Bookkeeping, YouTube tutorials and SEO. Competitors include Better Sheets itself, template sellers on Etsy and Gumroad, and bookkeeping tools like QuickBooks, Xero and Dext.
